claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae has a robust preference for fermentative glucose metabolism.
source: Robust preference for fermentative glucose metabolism has motivated domestication of the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about S. cerevisiae.

claim: The [GAR+] prion permits simultaneous metabolism of glucose and other carbon sources.
source: This program can be circumvented by a protein-based genetic element, the [GAR+] prion, permitting simultaneous metabolism of glucose and other carbon sources.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior work cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Diverse bacteria can elicit yeast cells to acquire [GAR+].
source: Diverse bacteria can elicit yeast cells to acquire [GAR+], although the molecular details of this interaction remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Jarosz et al., 2014a, 2014b).

claim: Lactic acid is a strong [GAR+] inducer.
source: Here we identify the common bacterial metabolite lactic acid as a strong [GAR+] inducer.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-5.

claim: Transient exposure to lactic acid caused yeast cells to heritably circumvent glucose repression.
source: Transient exposure to lactic acid caused yeast cells to heritably circumvent glucose repression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that cells exposed to lactic acid maintain the [GAR+] phenotype after propagation (Figure 5B).

claim: The lactic acid-induced trait had the defining genetic properties of [GAR+].
source: This trait had the defining genetic properties of [GAR+], and did not require utilization of lactic acid as a carbon source.
evidence: This is supported by data showing dominance in crosses, non-Mendelian inheritance, Hsp70 dependence, and PMA1 dependence (Figure 2).

claim: Lactic acid induction of [GAR+] did not require utilization of lactic acid as a carbon source.
source: This trait had the defining genetic properties of [GAR+], and did not require utilization of lactic acid as a carbon source.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that deletion of genes involved in lactic acid metabolism did not affect induction (Figure 3).

claim: Lactic acid induced [GAR+]-like epigenetic states in fungi that diverged from S. cerevisiae ~200 million years ago.
source: Lactic acid also induced [GAR+]-like epigenetic states in fungi that diverged from S. cerevisiae ~200 million years ago, and in which glucose repression evolved independently.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in D. bruxellensis (Figure 6).

claim: This is the first study to uncover a bacterial metabolite with the capacity to potently induce a prion.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study to uncover a bacterial metabolite with the capacity to potently induce a prion.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding, based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Small molecules commonly drive productive and destructive relationships between species.
source: Small molecules commonly drive productive and destructive relationships between species.
evidence: This is supported by citations to examples in the literature (Alegado et al., 2012; Ehrhardt et al., 1992; Hogan and Kolter, 2002; Hogan et al., 2004).

claim: Small molecule interactions between mammals and their associated gut microbiota may have important consequences for human health.
source: Small molecule interactions between mammals and their associated gut microbiota may have important consequences for human health (David et al., 2014; Lozupone et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cross-kingdom interactions have commercial relevance in the fermentation of alcoholic beverages.
source: Cross-kingdom interactions also have commercial relevance – for example those that occur between yeast and bacteria in the fermentation of alcoholic beverages (Bisson et al., 2007; Bokulich et al., 2012; Boulton et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Lactic acid bacteria are a common contaminant in incomplete fermentations.
source: Pasteur and others since have noted that lactic acid bacteria are a common contaminant in incomplete fermentations (Boulton et al., 1996; Pasteur, 1873).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical and modern literature.

claim: Some bacteria have the power to both reduce the ethanol content and spoil the taste profile of fermented beverages.
source: Indeed, brewers and vintners have long appreciated that some bacteria have the power to both reduce the ethanol content and spoil the taste profile of fermented beverages.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: S. cerevisiae strongly favors glucose as a carbon source even when other carbohydrates are present.
source: The budding yeast S. cerevisiae is a metabolic specialist: it strongly favors glucose as a carbon source even when other carbohydrates are present (Johnston, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Glucose-associated repression of metabolism is achieved through stringent regulation of enzymes involved in glycolysis and respiration at both the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
source: This is achieved through stringent regulation of enzymes involved in glycolysis and respiration at both the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels (Johnston, 1999; Zampar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Glucose-associated repression of metabolism is a defining feature of S. cerevisiae and many other microorganisms.
source: Such glucose-associated repression of metabolism is a defining feature of S. cerevisiae, and many other microorganisms (Gorke and Stulke, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A similar preference for glycolytic metabolism, even in the presence of oxygen, is a defining feature of cancer cells, known as the 'Warburg effect'.
source: A similar preference for glycolytic metabolism, even in the presence of oxygen, is a defining feature of cancer cells, known as the 'Warburg effect' (Hsu and Sabatini, 2008; Liberti and Locasale, 2016; Vander Heiden et al., 2009; Warburg, 1956).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When yeast cultures switch from metabolizing glucose to utilizing a respirative carbon source such as glycerol, they experience a pronounced lag phase known as the diauxic shift.
source: When yeast cultures switch from metabolizing glucose to utilizing a respirative carbon source such as glycerol, they experience a pronounced lag phase known as the diauxic shift.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast metabolism.

claim: The diauxic shift pause in growth occurs as a new transcriptional program is engaged to favor respiration.
source: This pause in growth occurs as a new transcriptional program is engaged to favor respiration (Galdieri et al., 2010; Zampar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Just 0.05% of the glucose mimetic glucosamine prevents yeast cells from utilizing non-fermentable carbon sources present at 40-fold higher concentrations.
source: For example, just 0.05% of the mimetic glucosamine prevents yeast cells from utilizing non-fermentable carbon sources present at 40-fold higher concentrations (Ball et al., 1976; Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Kunz and Ball, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Yeast strains have the ability to overcome glucose-associated repression of metabolism at frequencies that depend upon the ecological niche from which they were isolated.
source: We recently reported that yeast strains have the ability to overcome such glucose-associated repression of metabolism at frequencies that depend upon the ecological niche from which they were isolated (Jarosz et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: [GAR+] allows yeast to switch from being metabolic specialists to metabolic generalists, gaining the ability to metabolize a wide variety of carbon sources in the presence of glucose.
source: This allows them to switch from being metabolic specialists to metabolic generalists, gaining the ability to metabolize a wide variety of carbon sources in the presence of glucose.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: The heritable change in metabolic program associated with [GAR+] is not accompanied by a change in the yeast genotype.
source: This heritable change in metabolic program is not accompanied by a change in the yeast genotype.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of prions, supported by prior work.

claim: The [GAR+] trait is cytoplasmically transduced from mother cells to their daughters through the inheritance of an altered protein conformation.
source: Rather, the trait is cytoplasmically transduced from mother cells to their daughters through the inheritance of an altered protein conformation – a prion known as [GAR+] (named for its ability to reverse glucose associated repression) (Brown and Lindquist, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: [GAR+]'s nomenclature derives from defining characteristics of prion biology: dominance in genetic crosses (denoted by capital letters) and transmission to all progeny of meiosis (denoted by brackets).
source: [GAR+]'s nomenclature derives from defining characteristics of prion biology: dominance in genetic crosses (denoted by capital letters) and transmission to all progeny of meiosis (denoted by brackets).
evidence: This is an explanation of the nomenclature based on established prion biology conventions.

claim: The ability to acquire [GAR+] has been widely conserved among wild S. cerevisiae strains.
source: The ability to acquire [GAR+] has been widely conserved among wild S. cerevisiae strains and is also present in fungal species separated by at least two hundred million years of evolution (Jarosz et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ability to acquire [GAR+] is present in fungal species separated by at least two hundred million years of evolution.
source: The ability to acquire [GAR+] has been widely conserved among wild S. cerevisiae strains and is also present in fungal species separated by at least two hundred million years of evolution (Jarosz et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Under monoculture conditions in the laboratory, acquisition of [GAR+] occurs much more frequently than spontaneous mutations that reverse glucose repression.
source: Under monoculture conditions in the laboratory, acquisition of [GAR+] occurs much more frequently than spontaneous mutations that reverse glucose repression (Brown and Lindquist, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The precise rates of [GAR+] appearance correlate with environmental niche from which yeast are derived, suggestive of a bet-hedging mechanism for adaptation in environments with fluctuating carbon stores.
source: In nature, the precise rates of [GAR+] appearance correlate with environmental niche from which yeast are derived, suggestive of a bet-hedging mechanism for adaptation in environments with fluctuating carbon stores (Griswold and Masel, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014b; Lancaster and Masel, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: [GAR+] can be induced by cross-kingdom communication with many bacterial species.
source: Perhaps most remarkably, [GAR+] can be induced by cross-kingdom communication with many bacterial species, and this interaction has been conserved over long evolutionary timescales (Jarosz et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The bacterial induction of [GAR+] has been conserved over long evolutionary timescales.
source: Perhaps most remarkably, [GAR+] can be induced by cross-kingdom communication with many bacterial species, and this interaction has been conserved over long evolutionary timescales (Jarosz et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The relationship between bacteria and [GAR+] induction substantiates a model in which [GAR+]'s benefit as a reversible bet-hedging element would alone be sufficient to motivate its evolutionary retention.
source: Notably, this relationship substantiates a model in which [GAR+]'s benefit as a reversible bet-hedging element would alone be sufficient to motivate its evolutionary retention (Jarosz et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and represents an inference about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: Induction of [GAR+] by bacteria occurs with an extremely high efficiency – orders of magnitude greater than the spontaneous acquisition rate.
source: Induction of [GAR+] by bacteria occurs with an extremely high efficiency – orders of magnitude greater than the spontaneous acquisition rate – and the consequences are mutually beneficial.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: [GAR+] yeast cells gain the ability to metabolize a wider range of carbohydrates.
source: [GAR+] yeast cells gain the ability to metabolize a wider range of carbohydrates, improved uptake of limiting nutrients, and increased chronological lifespan (Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: [GAR+] yeast cells have improved uptake of limiting nutrients.
source: [GAR+] yeast cells gain the ability to metabolize a wider range of carbohydrates, improved uptake of limiting nutrients, and increased chronological lifespan (Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: [GAR+] yeast cells have increased chronological lifespan.
source: [GAR+] yeast cells gain the ability to metabolize a wider range of carbohydrates, improved uptake of limiting nutrients, and increased chronological lifespan (Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: [GAR+] yeast cells produce less ethanol.
source: [GAR+] yeast cells also produce less ethanol, which itself has anti-bacterial properties.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Ethanol has anti-bacterial properties.
source: [GAR+] yeast cells also produce less ethanol, which itself has anti-bacterial properties.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Reduced ethanol production by [GAR+] yeast generates a more hospitable environment for the inducing bacteria and allows them to flourish in fermentations where they would otherwise have perished.
source: This generates a more hospitable environment for the inducing bacteria and allows them to flourish in fermentations where they would otherwise have perished (Jarosz et al., 2014a); bacterial species that strongly induce [GAR+] are common contaminants in failed wine fermentations (Bisson et al., 2007; Boulton et al., 1996; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bacterial species that strongly induce [GAR+] are common contaminants in failed wine fermentations.
source: This generates a more hospitable environment for the inducing bacteria and allows them to flourish in fermentations where they would otherwise have perished (Jarosz et al., 2014a); bacterial species that strongly induce [GAR+] are common contaminants in failed wine fermentations (Bisson et al., 2007; Boulton et al., 1996; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When yeast and inducing bacteria are co-cultured on solid medium, induction of [GAR+] occurs along a spatial gradient emanating from the bacteria.
source: When yeast and inducing bacteria are co-cultured on solid medium, induction of [GAR+] occurs along a spatial gradient emanating from the bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Conditioned medium generated from cultures of inducing bacteria also induces the [GAR+] prion.
source: Conditioned medium generated from cultures of these bacteria also induces the prion (Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Inducing bacteria produce a diffusible signal that promotes [GAR+] in yeast.
source: These results and others have led us to propose that inducing bacteria produce a diffusible signal that promotes [GAR+] in yeast.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior experimental observations.

claim: Pre-treatment with conditioned medium from S. gallinarum caused naïve [gar−] yeast cells to grow robustly on GLY + GlcN.
source: Serial dilutions of naïve [gar−] yeast did not grow on GLY + GlcN alone over a five day period, but pre-treatment with the conditioned medium caused the yeast cells to grow robustly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pre-treatment with purified extract from S. gallinarum afforded growth to a similar degree as S. gallinarum itself.
source: Pre-treatment with this purified extract afforded growth to a similar degree as S. gallinarum itself (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: After two rounds of purification, the inducing activity eluted in a single fraction as a homogenous peak.
source: After these two rounds of purification, the inducing activity eluted in a single fraction as a homogenous peak.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from HPLC purification.

claim: NMR and mass spectrometry analyses revealed that the active fraction contained high concentrations of lactic acid.
source: We combined active fractions from multiple injections and analyzed this peak by NMR and mass spectrometry. Both analyses revealed that the active fraction contained high concentrations of lactic acid (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both L- and D- isomers of lactic acid strongly induce [GAR+] in a concentration dependent manner.
source: Plating assay (see Materials and methods) showing that both L- and D- isomers of lactic acid strongly induce [GAR+] in a concentration dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Lactic acid exists in two distinct forms: L-(+)-lactic acid (L-LA) and its mirror image D-(–)-lactic acid (D-LA).
source: Lactic acid, a small organic molecule, exists in two distinct forms: L-(+)-lactic acid (L-LA) and its mirror image D-(–)-lactic acid (D-LA).
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge.

claim: Some bacteria, including lactic acid bacteria (LAB), have the ability to produce one or both forms of lactic acid from carbohydrates.
source: Some bacteria, including the class known as lactic acid bacteria (LAB), have the ability to produce one or both forms from carbohydrates (Eiteman and Ramalingam, 2015; Salminen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Eukaryotes typically can metabolize both isomers of lactic acid, sometimes to varying degrees.
source: Eukaryotes typically can metabolize both isomers, sometimes to varying degrees (Adeva-Andany et al., 2014; Pajot and Claisse, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Malolactic fermentation by LAB in winemaking can typically yield up to 2.5 g/L of lactic acid, or 0.25%.
source: Malolactic fermentation by LAB in winemaking can typically yield up to 2.5 g/L of lactic acid, or 0.25% (Boulton et al., 1996); in other fermented foods, concentrations can exceed 10 g/L, or >1% (Fleming et al., 1988; Plengvidhya et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In some fermented foods, lactic acid concentrations can exceed 10 g/L, or >1%.
source: Malolactic fermentation by LAB in winemaking can typically yield up to 2.5 g/L of lactic acid, or 0.25% (Boulton et al., 1996); in other fermented foods, concentrations can exceed 10 g/L, or >1% (Fleming et al., 1988; Plengvidhya et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Many bacterial species that strongly induce [GAR+] are known LAB.
source: Moreover, many bacterial species that we previously found to strongly induce [GAR+] are known LAB (Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Addition of 0.05% lactic acid did not increase growth on YP alone.
source: Addition of 0.05% lactic acid did not increase growth on YP alone, eliminating the possibility that the yeast were simply metabolizing the lactic acid (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (not shown).

claim: Induction of [GAR+] by lactic acid was robust in synthetic complete medium.
source: Induction was also robust in synthetic complete medium, further establishing that it was due to the added lactic acid, rather than unknown components of the medium (e.g. yeast extract, peptone, or an unknown metabolite therein; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There were no significant prion-dependent differences in growth rates between [GAR+] cells and [gar−] cells in liquid YP-glycerol alone or in YP-glycerol supplemented with 0.35% lactic acid.
source: We did not observe any significant prion-dependent differences in growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), supporting an induction mechanism rather than selection of a pre-existing population.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The lack of growth rate differences between [GAR+] and [gar−] cells in the presence of lactic acid supports an induction mechanism rather than selection of a pre-existing population.
source: We did not observe any significant prion-dependent differences in growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), supporting an induction mechanism rather than selection of a pre-existing population.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.

claim: Glucose repression can be commonly circumvented in S. cerevisiae by induction of the [GAR+] prion.
source: Glucose repression can be commonly circumvented in S. cerevisiae by induction of the [GAR+] prion, but it can less frequently arise from genetic mutations (Ball et al., 1976; Kunz and Ball, 1977) and, in principle, from other heritable epigenetic modifications (Jarosz et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Glucose repression can less frequently arise from genetic mutations.
source: Glucose repression can be commonly circumvented in S. cerevisiae by induction of the [GAR+] prion, but it can less frequently arise from genetic mutations (Ball et al., 1976; Kunz and Ball, 1977) and, in principle, from other heritable epigenetic modifications (Jarosz et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: All diploids from crosses between lactic acid-induced cells and naïve isogenic mating partners grew on GLY + GlcN medium.
source: We first mated yeast cells that had been induced with 0.1% lactic acid to naïve isogenic mating partners and selected for diploids. All diploids we tested grew on GLY + GlcN medium, and moreover exhibited the same unusual pattern of semi-dominance (Figure 2A) – in which the diploid cells exhibit a strength of reversal of glucose repression that is intermediate between the two haploid parents – that is highly characteristic of both spontaneous and bacterially-induced [GAR+] (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Diploids from lactic acid-induced cells exhibited the same unusual pattern of semi-dominance that is highly characteristic of both spontaneous and bacterially-induced [GAR+].
source: All diploids we tested grew on GLY + GlcN medium, and moreover exhibited the same unusual pattern of semi-dominance (Figure 2A) – in which the diploid cells exhibit a strength of reversal of glucose repression that is intermediate between the two haploid parents – that is highly characteristic of both spontaneous and bacterially-induced [GAR+] (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citations to prior work.

claim: Nearly all spores from lactic acid-induced diploids (29 of 31) exhibited the [GAR+] phenotype.
source: We next sporulated diploid cells induced with lactic acid, dissected multiple tetrads, and examined the ability of the resulting spores to grow on GLY + GlcN. Nearly all spores we tested (29 of 31) exhibited the [GAR+] phenotype, in agreement with the non-Mendelian, dominant inheritance previously noted for both spontaneous and bacterially induced [GAR+] cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The inheritance pattern of lactic acid-induced [GAR+] is in agreement with the non-Mendelian, dominant inheritance previously noted for both spontaneous and bacterially induced [GAR+] cells.
source: Nearly all spores we tested (29 of 31) exhibited the [GAR+] phenotype, in agreement with the non-Mendelian, dominant inheritance previously noted for both spontaneous and bacterially induced [GAR+] cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior work.

claim: [GAR+] is unusual among known prions in that it is not influenced by perturbation of the Hsp104 disaggregase.
source: [GAR+] is unusual among known prions in that it is not influenced by perturbation of the Hsp104 disaggregase (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: [GAR+] is sensitive to perturbation of Hsp70 function.
source: Instead it is sensitive to perturbation of Hsp70 function (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Transient expression of a dominant negative Hsp70 variant cured multiple independent clones of their lactic acid-induced [GAR+] phenotype.
source: This regimen cured multiple independent clones of their induced [GAR+] phenotype, indicating that the lactic acid induced colonies have the same Hsp70-dependency as spontaneous and bacterially induced [GAR+] cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Lactic acid induced colonies have the same Hsp70-dependency as spontaneous and bacterially induced [GAR+] cells.
source: This regimen cured multiple independent clones of their induced [GAR+] phenotype, indicating that the lactic acid induced colonies have the same Hsp70-dependency as spontaneous and bacterially induced [GAR+] cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and comparison to prior work.

claim: Growing lactic acid-induced cells on plates containing the Hsp70 inhibitor myricetin reduced their ability to circumvent glucose repression.
source: We also grew induced cells on plates containing an Hsp70 inhibitor, myricetin (Chang et al., 2011; Koren et al., 2010), at concentrations that did not affect growth on GLY medium. This regimen, which has been shown to inhibit the growth of both spontaneous and bacterially induced [GAR+] on GLY + GlcN (Jarosz et al., 2014b), also reduced the ability of these colonies to circumvent glucose repression that had been induced by lactic acid (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PMA1 encodes the essential major plasma membrane proton pump in yeast.
source: PMA1 encodes the essential major plasma membrane proton pump in yeast; in [GAR+] cells Pma1 adopts an altered conformation and associates more strongly with another protein, Std1 (Brown and Lindquist, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In [GAR+] cells Pma1 adopts an altered conformation and associates more strongly with another protein, Std1.
source: PMA1 encodes the essential major plasma membrane proton pump in yeast; in [GAR+] cells Pma1 adopts an altered conformation and associates more strongly with another protein, Std1 (Brown and Lindquist, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cells harboring the pma1-DAmP allele had a low frequency of spontaneous prion acquisition.
source: Cells harboring this allele had a low frequency of spontaneous prion acquisition, and could not be induced to acquire [GAR+] by exposure to lactic acid (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cells harboring the pma1-DAmP allele could not be induced to acquire [GAR+] by exposure to lactic acid.
source: Cells harboring this allele had a low frequency of spontaneous prion acquisition, and could not be induced to acquire [GAR+] by exposure to lactic acid (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lactic acid can be imported into yeast via saturable ('active') and unsaturable ('passive') mechanisms.
source: Lactic acid can be imported into yeast via saturable ("active"') and unsaturable ('passive') mechanisms (Casal et al., 1999; Pacheco et al., 2012; Paiva et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both active and passive lactic acid import mechanisms depend upon the transcription factor SOK2.
source: Both depend upon the transcription factor SOK2, and the active mechanism is ultimately mediated by the monocarboxylate transporter JEN1.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The active lactic acid import mechanism is ultimately mediated by the monocarboxylate transporter JEN1.
source: Both depend upon the transcription factor SOK2, and the active mechanism is ultimately mediated by the monocarboxylate transporter JEN1.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Jen1 is required for yeast to grow on lactic acid as a sole carbon source.
source: Jen1 is required for yeast to grow on lactic acid as a sole carbon source, but is down-regulated during glucose repression (Casal et al., 1999; Pacheco et al., 2012), and its transcript was not abundant in [GAR+] cells compared to control cells (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Jen1 is down-regulated during glucose repression.
source: Jen1 is required for yeast to grow on lactic acid as a sole carbon source, but is down-regulated during glucose repression (Casal et al., 1999; Pacheco et al., 2012), and its transcript was not abundant in [GAR+] cells compared to control cells (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: JEN1 transcript was not abundant in [GAR+] cells compared to control cells.
source: Jen1 is required for yeast to grow on lactic acid as a sole carbon source, but is down-regulated during glucose repression (Casal et al., 1999; Pacheco et al., 2012), and its transcript was not abundant in [GAR+] cells compared to control cells (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of JEN1 greatly reduces growth on glycerol compared to wild-type cells.
source: Deletion of JEN1 greatly reduces growth on glycerol compared to wild-type cells, precluding its emergence in the previous screens for genes affecting [GAR+] (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of JEN1 did not influence [GAR+] induction by lactic acid at either low or high concentrations.
source: We therefore tested if lactic acid could induce jen1∆ cells to acquire [GAR+]. Deletion of JEN1 did not influence [GAR+] induction by lactic acid at either low or high concentrations (Figure 3A,B), indicating that active transport is not required.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Active transport of lactic acid is not required for [GAR+] induction.
source: Deletion of JEN1 did not influence [GAR+] induction by lactic acid at either low or high concentrations (Figure 3A,B), indicating that active transport is not required.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that deletion of JEN1 does not affect induction.

claim: Individual deletion of lactic acid dehydrogenases and transhydrogenases (DLD1, DLD2, DLD3, and CYB2) had no significant effect on [GAR+] induction by lactic acid.
source: We also tested whether enzymes reported to be involved in lactic acid metabolism in the Saccharomyces Genome Database (Cherry et al., 2012) could influence the ability of this molecule to induce [GAR+]. Individual deletion of these various lactic acid dehydrogenases and transhydrogenases (DLD1, DLD2, DLD3, and CYB2) also had no significant effect on [GAR+] induction by lactic acid (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The cellular mechanisms engaged by lactic acid to induce [GAR+] do not require its active import or its metabolism.
source: Thus, the cellular mechanisms engaged by lactic acid to induce [GAR+] do not require its active import or its metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that deletion of genes involved in lactic acid import and metabolism do not affect induction.

claim: SOK2 previously emerged as a hit in the screen for yeast mutants that were impaired in their ability to acquire [GAR+] upon induction by the bacterium Staphylococcus hominis.
source: SOK2 previously emerged as a hit in the screen for yeast mutants that were impaired in their ability to acquire [GAR+] upon induction by the bacterium Staphylococcus hominis (Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Yeast cells in which SOK2 was deleted were not induced by lactic acid.
source: We then tested whether loss of SOK2 impaired the capacity of lactic acid alone to induce [GAR+] in yeast cells. It did: yeast cells in which SOK2 was deleted were not induced by lactic acid (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The passive import of lactic acid is likely the dominant means through which this inducing signal is transmitted from bacteria to neighboring fungi.
source: Thus, the previously described passive import of lactic acid (Paiva et al., 2013) is likely the dominant means through which this inducing signal is transmitted from bacteria to neighboring fungi.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that SOK2 is required for induction and that active transport (via JEN1) is not required.

claim: Even the lowest concentration of lactic acid tested (0.015%) increased the number of colonies that arose on a GLY + GlcN plate by nearly three orders of magnitude.
source: Even the lowest concentration we tested in this experiment, 0.015%, increased the number of colonies that arose on a GLY + GlcN plate by nearly three orders of magnitude, such that approximately 5% of cells grew into medium-sized colonies (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing concentrations of lactic acid up to 0.25% did not strongly increase the degree of [GAR+] induction.
source: Increasing concentrations of lactic acid up to 0.25% did not strongly increase the degree of induction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 1% lactic acid caused an even stronger induction, such that nearly all cells in the population grew into large colonies on GLY + GlcN media.
source: However, 1% lactic acid caused an even stronger induction, such that nearly all cells in the population grew into large colonies on GLY + GlcN media (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: [GAR+] can exist in multiple 'strains' – different heritable and stable activity states.
source: Like virtually all prions, [GAR+] can exist in multiple 'strains' – different heritable and stable activity states.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: When [GAR+] colonies arise spontaneously on selective GLY + GlcN plates, 'strong' [GAR+] colonies are larger than 'weak' [GAR+] colonies.
source: When they arise spontaneously on selective GLY + GlcN plates, 'strong' [GAR+] colonies are larger than 'weak' [GAR+] colonies (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both 'strong' and 'weak' [GAR+] activity states are heritable over long biological timescales.
source: Both activity states are heritable over long biological timescales (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Jarosz et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Small colonies induced with low concentrations of lactic acid grew modestly on GLY + GlcN after propagation, in a manner that mimicked 'weak' [GAR+] strains.
source: The small colonies that had originally been induced with low concentrations of lactic acid grew modestly on GLY + GlcN, in a manner that mimicked 'weak' [GAR+] strains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Large colonies induced with high concentrations of lactic acid grew robustly on GLY + GlcN after propagation, in a manner that mimicked 'strong' [GAR+] strains.
source: The large colonies that had originally been induced with high concentrations of lactic acid grew robustly on GLY + GlcN, in a manner that mimicked 'strong' [GAR+] strains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Alterations in the concentration of lactic acid produced by inducing bacteria may engage different heritable activity states, or so-called 'strains', of the [GAR+] prion.
source: Thus, alterations in the concentration of lactic acid produced by inducing bacteria may engage different heritable activity states, or so-called 'strains', of the [GAR+] prion.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that different concentrations of lactic acid induce different strengths of [GAR+].

claim: Glucose repression has evolved multiple times in the fungal lineage.
source: Glucose repression has evolved multiple times in the fungal lineage (Hagman and Piskur, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dekkera bruxellensis diverged from S. cerevisiae 200 million years ago.
source: Dekkera bruxellensis, an organism used in the production of lambic beers that diverged from S. cerevisiae 200 million years ago, uses a distinct mechanism for engaging stringent glucose repression (Rozpedowska et al., 2011; Woolfit et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: D. bruxellensis uses a distinct mechanism for engaging stringent glucose repression.
source: Dekkera bruxellensis, an organism used in the production of lambic beers that diverged from S. cerevisiae 200 million years ago, uses a distinct mechanism for engaging stringent glucose repression (Rozpedowska et al., 2011; Woolfit et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: D. bruxellensis can spontaneously acquire a [GAR+]-like state to become a metabolic generalist.
source: We previously established that despite this evolutionary distance, D. bruxellensis can spontaneously acquire a [GAR+]-like state to become a metabolic generalist (Jarosz et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The [GAR+]-like state in D. bruxellensis can be induced by cross-kingdom chemical communication with bacteria.
source: This [GAR+]-like state can also be induced by cross-kingdom chemical communication with bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Concentrations of lactic acid well within the physiological range produced by bacteria (0.02%) induced robust growth of D. bruxellensis on GLY + GlcN.
source: We exposed naïve D. bruxellensis strains to lactic acid, guided by our results from S. cerevisiae. Concentrations well within the physiological range of lactic acid produced by bacteria (0.02%) induced robust growth on GLY + GlcN (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Lactic acid-induced D. bruxellensis colonies maintained the ability to circumvent glucose repression after propagation for ~75 generations on non-selective rich medium.
source: We picked colonies from these selections and propagated them for ~75 generations on non-selective rich medium (YPD). In each case, the trait was heritable: induced colonies maintained the ability to circumvent glucose repression (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The [GAR+]-like states that arise spontaneously or are induced by bacteria in D. bruxellensis depend strongly on the activity of Hsp70 chaperones.
source: The [GAR+]-like states that arise spontaneously or are induced by bacteria in D. bruxellensis depend strongly on the activity of Hsp70 chaperones (Jarosz et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Hsp70 inhibitor myricetin significantly reduced the ability of lactic acid-induced D. bruxellensis colonies to circumvent glucose repression.
source: This treatment significantly reduced the ability of these induced colonies to circumvent glucose repression (Figure 6B), just as it does for the [GAR+]-like states that arise spontaneously in this organism (Jarosz et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Across a vast evolutionary distance, bacterial production of lactic acid can engage [GAR+]-like mechanisms to heritably convert neighboring fungi from metabolic specialists to metabolic generalists.
source: Thus, across a vast evolutionary distance, bacterial production of lactic acid can engage [GAR+]-like mechanisms to heritably convert neighboring fungi from metabolic specialists to metabolic generalists.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that lactic acid induces [GAR+]-like states in both S. cerevisiae and D. bruxellensis.

claim: The ability of lactic acid to elicit the [GAR+] prion could provide a molecular mechanism for Pasteur's observations about lactic acid producing bacteria leading to fermentation failure.
source: More than a century ago, Louis Pasteur documented what vintners have long since appreciated: the presence of lactic acid producing bacteria in fermentations can often lead to their failure (Pasteur, 1873). Our observations suggest that the ability of lactic acid to elicit the [GAR+] prion could provide a molecular mechanism for those observations.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and historical observations.

claim: The [GAR+] prion can confer strong selective advantage – converting metabolic specialists to metabolic generalists in a manner that improves fitness in complex microbial communities.
source: The [GAR+] prion is found in evolutionarily distant fungal species, and can confer strong selective advantage – converting metabolic specialists to metabolic generalists in a manner that improves fitness in complex microbial communities (Jarosz et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recent evidence points to important signaling roles for lactic acid in human cancer cells, in the context of the Warburg effect.
source: Recent evidence points to important signaling roles for lactic acid in human cancer cells, in the context of the Warburg effect (Adeva-Andany et al., 2014; Dhup et al., 2012; Fiaschi et al., 2012; Liberti and Locasale, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Other studies have linked LAB to benefits for human health and disease prevention.
source: Other studies have linked LAB to benefits for human health and disease prevention, however it remains unclear how much these effects are due to the effects of lactic acid on host cells (Kim et al., 2007; Masood et al., 2011; Tiptiri-Kourpeti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In at least some cases, LAB appear to exert their health effects by influencing other microbes, for example, modulating the virulence of Clostridium difficile.
source: In at least some cases, LAB appear to exert their health effects by influencing other microbes, for example, modulating the virulence of Clostridium difficile (Lee et al., 2013; Yun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The discovery of a connection between passive lactic acid uptake and the ability to induce [GAR+] (via SOK2) provides new insight into the initiation of this complex cross-kingdom chemical communication.
source: Our discovery of a connection between passive lactic acid uptake and the ability to induce [GAR+] (via our results with SOK2) provides new insight into the initiation of this complex cross-kingdom chemical communication.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that SOK2 is required for induction.

claim: Other molecules may modulate [GAR+] induction by lactic acid.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that other molecules may modulate [GAR+] induction by lactic acid.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations about differences in induction kinetics and species-specificity.

claim: The kinetics of [GAR+] induction were slightly faster in conditioned media than with lactic acid alone.
source: Although we were able to fully reconstitute induction with lactic acid alone, the kinetics were slightly faster in conditioned media.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Some of the bacteria that induce [GAR+] in S. cerevisiae do not induce the [GAR+]-like state in D. bruxellensis, even though high levels of lactic acid can induce the prion in each of these organisms.
source: Moreover, some of the bacteria that induce [GAR+] in S. cerevisiae do not induce the [GAR+]-like state in D. bruxellensis, even though high levels of lactic acid can induce the prion in each of these organisms.
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: Other bacterially secreted factors may influence perception of the lactic acid signal, and the effects of these molecules may be species specific.
source: An intriguing but plausible explanation is that other bacterially secreted factors influence perception of the lactic acid signal, and that the effects of these molecules may also be species specific.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations about species-specific differences in bacterial induction.

claim: There is precedent for multiple bacterially secreted molecules being required for full induction of developmental changes in choanoflagellates.
source: Indeed, there is precedent for this behavior in choanoflagellates, where two bacterially secreted lipids were required to recapitulate full induction of rosette, multicellular colony formation (Alegado et al., 2012; Woznica et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is possible that other molecules could also fuel the cross-kingdom interaction that induces [GAR+] in diverse ecological niches.
source: Finally, although we have shown that S. gallinarium induces [GAR+] via lactic acid, it is entirely possible that other molecules could also fuel this cross-kingdom interaction in diverse ecological niches.
evidence: This is speculation about the possibility of other inducing molecules.

claim: There is precedent in mechanisms of quorum sensing for competition among inducers secreted by different bacteria.
source: There is also precedent in mechanisms of quorum sensing for competition among inducers secreted by different bacteria (Drescher et al., 2014; Even-Tov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Other prion-like epigenetic states could be regulated by common metabolites, at times in service of cross-species communication.
source: Perhaps most remarkably, our study raises the possibility that other prion-like epigenetic states could be regulated by common metabolites, at times in service of cross-species communication.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of this study.

claim: General stressors that perturb protein homeostasis can modestly elevate the frequency of cells harboring the [PSI+] or [MOT3+] prions.
source: Prior studies have highlighted the fact that general stressors that perturb protein homeostasis can modestly elevate the frequency of cells harboring the [PSI+] or [MOT3+] prions (Holmes et al., 2013; Tyedmers et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Intrinsic links between stress responses and prion switching ensure that subpopulations of cells can diversify their phenotypes when they are ill-suited to the environment.
source: These intrinsic links between stress responses and prion switching ensure that subpopulations of cells can diversify their phenotypes when they are ill-suited to the environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work about stress-induced prion switching.

claim: The findings extend prion biology to a more concerted, switch-like behavior in which prions can serve as a target for rapid and effective cross-species communication.
source: Our findings extend this biology to a more concerted, switch-like behavior in which prions can serve as a target for rapid and effective cross-species communication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Biological niches like the human body harbor microbial communities that are far more complex than those studied in this work.
source: Biological niches like the human body harbor microbial communities that are far more complex than those we have studied here (Lozupone et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The robust connection between lactic acid and a heritable change in metabolic strategy has been missed despite a multitude of studies in S. cerevisiae.
source: It is striking that the robust connection we have discovered between a simple metabolite and a heritable change in metabolic strategy has been missed despite a multitude studies in this model organism.
evidence: This is an observation about the novelty of the finding.

claim: The observations underscore the potential of cross-kingdom molecular communication to illuminate biological processes, in particular its capacity to elicit heritable, epigenetic transformations of biological traits.
source: Our observations thus underscore the potential of cross-kingdom molecular communication to illuminate biological processes, in particular its capacity to elicit heritable, epigenetic transformations of biological traits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.
